query_text: Write the history of a colour.

content.text:
## A Short History of Blue

Blue feels ancient: the colour of sky, sea, distance, calm, divinity, melancholy, and trust. But as a human-made colour — as pigment, dye, symbol, and social category — blue had a surprisingly uneven history.

For much of early human history, blue was difficult to capture. Earth naturally offers reds, browns, yellows, and blacks in ochres, charcoal, and minerals, so prehistoric art is rich in those colours. Blue, by contrast, was rarer in stable pigments. The sky and water were everywhere, but turning “blueness” into paint or cloth was hard.

One of the earliest major blue pigments was **Egyptian blue**, developed in ancient Egypt around the third millennium BCE. It was a synthetic pigment made by heating silica, copper compounds, lime, and an alkali. The result was a brilliant blue material used in wall paintings, sculpture, ceramics, and funerary objects. To the Egyptians, blue evoked the Nile, the heavens, fertility, rebirth, and divine protection.

Another treasured blue came from **lapis lazuli**, a deep blue stone mined especially in what is now Afghanistan. Ground into pigment, it became **ultramarine**, literally “from beyond the sea” in medieval Europe. It was extraordinarily expensive — sometimes more costly than gold — and was therefore reserved for sacred and prestigious images. In Christian art, ultramarine became closely associated with the robes of the Virgin Mary, giving blue a powerful aura of holiness, purity, and importance.

Yet blue was not always culturally dominant. In ancient Greek and Roman literature, blue seems less central than white, black, red, and gold. Some scholars have noted that ancient colour vocabularies did not always divide the spectrum as modern English does. Colours were often described by brightness, texture, shine, or darkness as much as by hue. The absence of a familiar “blue” word in some ancient texts does not mean people could not see blue; it means they organized colour differently.

In Europe during the early Middle Ages, blue was sometimes a modest or secondary colour. That changed between the 12th and 13th centuries. The cult of the Virgin Mary, stained-glass windows, heraldry, and royal symbolism helped elevate blue’s status. French kings adopted blue decorated with golden fleurs-de-lis, and blue gradually became a colour of nobility, loyalty, and spiritual authority.

Blue also entered daily life through dye. The main European source was **woad**, a plant that produced a blue dye after fermentation. In Asia and later across global trade routes, **indigo** became the more powerful blue dye. Indigo was richer, more concentrated, and eventually more commercially important than woad. Its history is also tied to colonialism, plantation labour, and enslavement, especially in parts of the Caribbean and the American South. The beauty of blue cloth often carried a hidden history of exploitation.

The 18th century brought a revolution in blue pigments. Around 1704, **Prussian blue** was accidentally discovered in Berlin. It was the first modern synthetic blue pigment, cheaper than ultramarine and intense enough to transform painting, printing, textiles, and decorative arts. Artists could now use strong blue more freely. Later, synthetic ultramarine and cobalt blue expanded the palette even further.

By the 19th century, blue had become deeply embedded in modern culture. Dark blue uniforms suggested discipline and authority. Navy blue belonged to sailors, police, and institutions. Blue also became the colour of workwear: indigo-dyed denim, first valued for durability, eventually became the fabric of miners, cowboys, rebels, teenagers, and global fashion.

Emotionally, blue developed two seemingly opposite meanings. On one hand, it suggested serenity, truth, loyalty, and stability — the reason banks, governments, and technology companies still use it so often. On the other hand, “the blues” came to mean sadness, longing, and a musical tradition born from African American experience. Blue could be heavenly or sorrowful, official or rebellious, distant or intimate.

Today, blue is one of the world’s most popular colours. It appears on national flags, corporate logos, jeans, hospital walls, religious images, social media apps, and environmental campaigns. It is the colour of planet Earth seen from space, yet also a colour humans spent millennia struggling to manufacture.

The history of blue is therefore a history of desire: the desire to possess the sky, to dye cloth with depth, to honour gods and saints, to signal power, to sell trust, and to give shape to sadness. Blue began as something almost unreachable — visible everywhere, but hard to hold. Over time, humans learned not only to make it, but to fill it with meaning.
